newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian navy speeds to yachtsmen's rescue.
newsitem.headline: Australian navy speeds to yachtsmen's rescue.

text.p: Australian rescuers held out hope on Wednesday for the survival of a British solo yachtsman as a navy frigate steamed towards the Antarctic where a second solo sailor waited to be plucked from a life raft.

The Royal Australian Navy frigate, HMAS Adelaide, hoped to launch a Seahawk helicopter at first light on Thursday to pick up French yachtsman Thierry Dubois from a life raft, its captain Raydon Gates said in a radio interview late on Wednesday night.

Rescuers then hope to head south to another area where they believe Tony Bullimore, 56, may be inside the hull of his upturned yacht, Global Exide Challenger, although listening devices dropped into the sea on Wednesday failed to pick up any signs of life.
"We are disappointed we haven't heard anything, but we are very hopeful we will hear," Australian Defence Force spokesman Colonel Andrew Reynolds told Reuters.
"It does not mean because we have not heard...that he is not there or that he is dead."

Bullimore and 29-year-old Dubois, competitors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race, capsized in wild seas on Sunday after hitting a storm about 900 miles from Antarctica and 1,400 miles from the Australian coast.
Dubois was found by a rescue plane a day later clinging to the upturned hull of his yacht Pour Amnesty International and managed to scramble aboard a life raft dropped from the air.
Bullimore has not been sighted but hopes for his safety were raised on Tuesday when one of his two distress beacons was switched to alert status, an operation that can only be done manually.
Gates said a bid to lift Dubois from his raft by helicopter late on Wednesday had been postponed due to low cloud and freezing conditions which made it unsafe to fly.
He told Reuters that a helicopter rescue would be attempted at first light on Thursday, although weather conditions had deteriorated, with 50 knot winds and five metre seas.
If conditions were unsafe for the helicopter, a boat would be launched later from the the frigate to try to reach Dubois.
"He is dry, which is very important," Gates said. "His spirits are down a bit obviously as the nights crawl on but he is aware that we are going to pick him up tomorrow morning."
HMAS Adelaide would then head 60 miles south to Bullimore's yacht, but could spend only 12 hours in the search zone.
Gates said the yacht's manufacturers had told the navy that Bullimore could survive reasonably well in the yacht's two living spaces and would have about 140 hours of air.
"If he's in his anti-immersion suit and he is out of the water in that upturned yacht he has a reasonable chance of still being alive when I reach him," he said.
Gates's optimism was at odds with a statement by acting Defence Minister Bronwyn Bishop early on Wednesday.
She said that defence officials then believed that Bullimore might have been attached to a rescue beacon that was known to have drifted away from his yacht.
Rescuers would try to establish contact with Bullimore through the hull so he could swim out, or would attempt to cut a hole into the yacht, Gates said.
But he did not play down the difficulties of recovering the yachtsmen in the turbulent sub-Antarctic waters.
"This is the furthest south we've ever had to effect a rescue," he said in the radio interview late on Wednesday.
The two yachtsmen were the latest competitors in the Vendee Globe round-the-world race to hit disaster in the stormy seas south of Australia.
Frenchman Rafael Dinelli, 28, arrived in Hobart, Tasmania, earlier on Wednesday after he was rescued from a life raft by a fellow competitor two days after Christmas.
